related.why: Bile duct injury as a specific risk

brief.scenario: A cholecystectomy specimen has been sent to the laboratory. The examiner will read out the histology from the gallbladder wall during the station. Written findings: the gallbladder has been opened along its length. The wall is diffusely thickened, firm and grey-white on cut section. The mucosa is flattened, with loss of its normal fine folds. The lumen contains numerous small stones, each a few millimetres across, faceted where they press against one another, and yellow-brown. No stone is impacted in Hartmann's pouch, and no discrete mass is seen in the wall.
brief.task: Summarise and interpret the written specimen findings and the histology the examiner reads out, and answer questions on gallstone disease and its complications.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Summarise the wall and the stones, then work outwards: gallbladder, ducts, pancreas, bowel.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Relying on Murphy's sign alone to diagnose acute cholecystitis.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "This is an opened gallbladder containing multiple stones."

grid.label: Specimen summary
grid.fail: Says "gallstones" without summarising the wall or the stones.
grid.pass: Opened gallbladder: summarises wall thickness, mucosa, and the stones' number, size, shape and colour.
grid.high: Recognises chronic inflammation (thick fibrotic wall) and comments on Hartmann's pouch and any wall mass.

grid.label: Stone types
grid.pass: Cholesterol, pigment (black or brown) and mixed stones.
grid.high: Links each to its cause: cholesterol supersaturation; black with haemolysis or cirrhosis; brown with biliary infection.

grid.label: Histology
grid.fail: Cannot tell acute from chronic inflammation.
grid.pass: Acute: oedema, neutrophils, mucosal ulceration. Chronic: fibrosis, chronic inflammatory cells, Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses.
grid.high: Explains Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses as mucosa herniating through the muscle wall under raised pressure.

grid.label: Complications
grid.fail: Cannot name a complication outside the gallbladder.
grid.pass: Empyema, duct stones with cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis and gallstone ileus.
grid.high: Explains Mirizzi syndrome: a Hartmann's pouch stone compressing the common hepatic duct, raising the risk of duct injury at surgery.

grid.label: Diagnosis and severity
grid.pass: Diagnosis needs local signs, systemic inflammation and imaging findings (Tokyo Guidelines 2018).
grid.high: Grades severity: grade III with organ dysfunction; grade II with WCC over 18,000/mm³, a tender RUQ mass, or symptoms over 72 hours.

grid.label: Management
grid.borderline: Knows early surgery is preferred but gives no time frame.
grid.pass: Ultrasound and LFTs; early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 1 week of diagnosis.
grid.high: Adds MRCP when ultrasound misses duct stones but the duct is dilated or LFTs abnormal, and cholecystostomy for empyema if surgery is contraindicated.

grid.label: Safe conclusions
grid.fail: Calls it benign from the naked-eye findings alone, without histology.
grid.pass: States that histology confirms the diagnosis and excludes an incidental carcinoma.
grid.high: Commits to a most likely diagnosis while naming what would change it.

knowledge.fact: Acute cholecystitis: offer early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 1 week of diagnosis.
MRCP if ultrasound hasn't shown duct stones but the duct is dilated or LFTs are abnormal.
Tokyo 2018 grade II: WCC over 18,000/mm³, tender RUQ mass, symptoms over 72 hours, or marked local inflammation.
Charcot's triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) suggests cholangitis.
Mirizzi syndrome: a Hartmann's pouch stone compresses the common hepatic duct.

partner.opening: You have the written findings for a cholecystectomy specimen. Summarise them for me.

reveals.finding: Read out: the H&E section shows the gallbladder wall thickened by fibrous tissue, with scattered lymphocytes and plasma cells. Pockets of mucosal epithelium extend deep through the muscle layer into the wall. There are no sheets of neutrophils and no ulceration. Ask what this shows.
Give the clinical picture: 4 days of pain, WCC 19,000/mm³, no organ dysfunction.

curveballs.prompt: She is too frail for surgery and has an empyema. What now?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Percutaneous cholecystostomy if conservative management fails.

curveballs.prompt: Ultrasound shows a dilated duct but no stones. Next test?
The histology report mentions a focus of dysplasia. Does that change anything?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Yes: it needs discussion at the MDT, because the specimen is no longer simply benign.
